title: Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
ground_truth_notes: External award-winning paper. NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper (Datasets and Benchmarks track). Large-scale study of LM output diversity with INFINITY-CHAT benchmark. No insider commentary.

evidence.openreview_pdf: data/openreviews/public_slice/Artificial Hivemind_ The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond) _ OpenReview.pdf

official_concerns.text: The dataset is limited to English-language queries from WildChat, constraining the generalizability of findings across cultures and languages.
The paper provides limited actionable guidance on how to apply the Artificial Hivemind metric for model development or training feedback.

The analysis does not provide sufficient insight into the underlying causes of inter-model homogenization; the paper diagnoses the phenomenon but does not mechanistically disentangle causes like shared training data, alignment, or decoding.

The Artificial Hivemind phenomenon may be statistically expected given shared training data and the law of large numbers; autoregressive LMs are designed to approximate the average behavior, so cross-model similarity is a natural consequence rather than a surprising finding.

The homogenization findings should be tested with paraphrased versions of queries to verify whether the effect is robust to surface-level prompt variation, or whether models are simply responding to specific phrasings.
The impact of the open-ended query's entropy/difficulty on the strength of the Hivemind effect should be analyzed; less definitive questions may show different patterns than highly open-ended ones.
Figure 1 could be more concise; the visual presentation with many models is cluttered.
The paper should add discussion of the taxonomy problem in related works, connecting to prior work on open-endedness taxonomies.

The extent of the 'open-endedness' of collected queries was not verified; the dataset construction relies on automated filtering but lacks human validation that queries genuinely admit multiple plausible responses.

The cosine similarity scores used to demonstrate homogeneity lack a reference baseline or contextualization; without knowing what random or expected similarity looks like, the reported scores (0.7-0.8 range) cannot be meaningfully interpreted.

The analysis correlating model ratings with human ratings in Section 4 is technically flawed: the methodology for selecting 'similar-quality' responses and 'high annotator disagreement' subsets is questionable, the use of entropy as a disagreement measure is unjustified, and the motivation for averaging human ratings is unclear.

In Figure 6, most average similarity scores are tightly clustered in the 0.7-0.8 range with little difference among them, making it hard to meaningfully compare the numbers; full distributions rather than just averages should be shown.

If the goal is to compare inter- and intra-model similarity, why not use the cosine similarity as done in Figure 4 and 6/7 directly, instead of the different metric used for inter vs intra comparison?
The dataset link in the paper was broken at time of review; code is available but data was not accessible.

The testbed needs further validation by designing experiments on foundation models without instruction-following capabilities, to determine whether post-training (not just pretraining) drives the Hivemind effect.
The codebase would benefit from including scripts for testing each model candidate, so readers can reproduce the analysis and understand system prompt impact.
The new human annotation results introduced in the rebuttal should be fully included in the camera-ready version to strengthen the grounding and definition of open-endedness.
The results would benefit from deeper interpretation and discussion beyond reporting the observations.
The justification for using average human ratings as the ground truth for correlation analysis is unclear; annotator disagreement should be taken into account rather than averaged away.

decision_drivers.text: Core diversity measurement relies on a single unvalidated embedding model (text-embedding-3-small) without alternative metric triangulation.
No human diversity baseline makes the claim that LMs are 'too homogeneous' empirically ungrounded.
Paper framing of AI safety risks and homogenization of human thought overstates what the evidence supports.

mentions.text: Addresses an important and timely problem with implications for creativity and pluralistic alignment.
Impressive scale: 70+ models evaluated, 26K queries mined, 31K+ human annotations with 25 annotators per item.
The inter-model homogeneity analysis is novel — first systematic cross-model convergence analysis on real-world open-ended queries.
Well-constructed taxonomy of open-ended query types grounded in naturally occurring user interactions.
Compelling qualitative examples (e.g., Figure 1 showing 25 models collapsing into two metaphor clusters).
Thorough appendix with extensive model-level breakdowns, annotation interface, and paraphrase experiments.

agentic_concerns.text: The entire diversity measurement framework relies on cosine similarity from a single embedding model (text-embedding-3-small), never validated against human diversity judgments, with no alternative metrics explored.

No human diversity baseline is provided; without measuring pairwise similarity among human-authored responses, the claim that LMs are 'too homogeneous' cannot distinguish model convergence from task-inherent constraints.
Core experimental analyses use only 100 queries (intra/inter-model) and 50 queries (human annotation) from a pool of 26K, significantly limiting generalizability without adequate justification.

Section 4 findings are partly expected by construction: model-human correlation naturally drops in restricted-range (similar-quality) and high-noise (high-disagreement) subsets, and the paper does not control for this statistical artifact.
No causal analysis of why homogeneity occurs; the paper cannot distinguish shared training data, RLHF alignment, memorization, task constraints, or embedding artifacts as drivers.
The quality-diversity tradeoff is not studied; diversity is measured at a single decoding configuration without assessing whether more diverse outputs maintain acceptable quality.

The framing ('Artificial Hivemind,' 'long-term AI safety risks,' 'homogenization of human thought') is stronger than the evidence supports; the paper measures output similarity but provides no evidence of downstream impact on human creativity or behavior.

edges.issue: No causal analysis of why inter-model homogenization occurs
edges.rationale: Both identify that the paper diagnoses the Hivemind phenomenon but does not mechanistically disentangle potential causes (shared training data, alignment, decoding). O3 verbatim: 'does not clearly provide sufficient insights into the underlying causes.' A5: 'cannot distinguish shared training data, RLHF alignment, memorization.' Same specific gap.

edges.issue: Similarity scores lack a reference baseline for meaningful interpretation
edges.rationale: Both flag missing baselines for interpreting cosine similarity scores. O10 requests a random/expected similarity baseline (resolved in rebuttal with random pairs at 0.1-0.2 range). A2 requests a human diversity baseline (pairwise similarity among human-authored responses). Different reference points but same underlying gap: similarity values are uninterpretable without context. Partial because the specific baselines requested differ and would require different fixes.

edges.issue: Section 4 correlation analysis between model and human ratings has methodological flaws
edges.rationale: Both identify Section 4 methodology as problematic. O11 is broader: questions subset selection methods, entropy as disagreement measure, and motivation for averaging human ratings. A4 is narrower: specifically flags restricted-range effects as a statistical artifact in similar-quality and high-disagreement subsets. A4 captures one facet of O11's broader concern.

edges.issue: Whether the Hivemind finding is significant enough to warrant the paper's claims
edges.rationale: O4 challenges whether the Hivemind effect is truly surprising (statistically expected from shared training data and law of large numbers). A7 challenges whether the framing overstates the evidence (safety risks, human thought homogenization). Both question the paper's significance but from different angles: O4 is a conceptual/novelty challenge, A7 is an overclaiming/framing critique. Different issues despite thematic proximity.

decision_drivers.text: The Artificial Hivemind framing may oversimplify the scope of creativity and diversity in language models.
No empirical validation is provided for proposed mitigative strategies.

mentions.text: Novel dataset addressing a gap in evaluating language model diversity.
Comprehensive taxonomy covering diverse query types.
Extensive human-annotated data for preference analysis.

agentic_concerns.text: The dataset is limited to English queries, lacking multi-lingual analysis, which constrains generalizability.
Assumptions on the Artificial Hivemind effect may oversimplify the scope of creativity and diversity, reducing a complex phenomenon to a narrow framing.
The paper lacks empirical validation for proposed mitigative strategies against the homogenization phenomenon.
It is unclear how the human annotation insights directly inform mitigation strategies for the Hivemind effect.

edges.issue: English-only dataset limits generalizability across languages and cultures
edges.rationale: Both identify the same limitation: INFINITY-CHAT is restricted to English queries from WildChat, constraining cross-linguistic generalizability. Same scope, same severity.

edges.issue: Gap between diagnosing the Hivemind effect and providing actionable mitigation
edges.rationale: O2 flags limited actionable guidance on applying the metric; A3 flags missing empirical validation of mitigation strategies. Both target the diagnosis-to-action gap but from different angles: O2 is about how to use the metric, A3 is about whether mitigations work. Agentic rates major vs official moderate.

edges.issue: Unclear how the paper's insights translate to practical mitigation
edges.rationale: O2 asks for more actionable guidance on using the Hivemind metric; A4 asks how human annotation insights inform mitigation. Both target the same actionability gap from different facets. A4 specifically questions the annotation→mitigation link.

edges.issue: Conceptual challenge to the significance of the Hivemind finding
edges.rationale: Both challenge the paper's core conceptual framing but target different aspects. O4 argues homogeneity is statistically expected (not surprising); A2 argues the framing oversimplifies creativity scope. Related but not the same specific complaint — O4 is about statistical inevitability, A2 is about reductive framing.

decision_drivers.text: Sole reliance on sentence-embedding cosine similarity as the diversity metric without validation against human diversity judgments; conflates semantic similarity with lack of diversity.
Causal analysis of inter-model homogenization is entirely absent; the paper is purely descriptive without controlled experiments to disentangle contributing factors.
Human annotation study (Section 4) is disconnected from the diversity analysis (Section 3) and its conclusions may reflect a statistical artifact rather than meaningful calibration failure.

mentions.text: Scale and comprehensiveness of the empirical study: 70+ models evaluated across open-source and closed-source families with 50 samples per query per model, providing the most extensive cross-model diversity analysis to date.

High-quality dataset and annotation effort: INFINITY-CHAT fills a genuine gap with 25 annotations per example enabling distributional analysis of human preferences; taxonomy grounded in real WildChat user behavior.
Actionable downstream findings: demonstration that reward models and LM judges are poorly calibrated on similar-quality and high-disagreement subsets has direct implications for RLHF pipelines.
Thorough experimental design with robustness checks: multiple subset selection methods, alternative decoding strategies, paraphrase robustness experiments, and human validation of open-endedness.

agentic_concerns.text: Reliance on sentence embeddings (text-embedding-3-small) as the sole diversity metric without validation against human diversity judgments; cosine similarity conflates semantic similarity with lack of diversity, and the choice of embedding model is not justified or ablated.

Causal analysis of inter-model homogenization is entirely absent; the paper does not include even partial investigation (e.g., base vs. instruction-tuned, models on disjoint corpora) to distinguish benign convergence from problematic homogenization.

Human annotation study (Section 4) is disconnected from the diversity analysis (Section 3); the finding that model ratings correlate less on similar-quality subsets may be a statistical artifact (reduced variance, regression to the mean) rather than meaningful calibration failure, and the sample size (50 queries) is small.

Taxonomy and dataset construction rely heavily on GPT-4o with limited validation: 74.7% human-GPT-4o agreement on taxonomy labels is moderate, inter-annotator agreement among humans is not reported, and the open-endedness validation uses only 3 annotators per query on 100 examples.

Conceptual novelty is incremental: the observation that LMs lack diversity is well-documented, and the paper primarily scales up and systematizes existing intuitions rather than introducing fundamentally new analytical frameworks or mitigation strategies.

edges.issue: Embedding-based similarity metric lacks proper grounding for interpreting diversity
edges.rationale: Both flag inadequacy of the cosine similarity metric. O10 specifically asks for a reference baseline to interpret scores; A1 is broader, questioning the metric's validity against human diversity judgments and the choice of embedding model. A1 encompasses O10's concern but goes further — fixing O10 (adding a random baseline) would not fully address A1 (human validation of the metric). Partial because A1 is strictly broader in scope.

edges.issue: Embedding similarity scores do not meaningfully differentiate models
edges.rationale: O12 raises the narrow clustering of scores (0.7-0.8) making comparison difficult; A1 questions whether the metric captures diversity at all. Both point to limitations of the cosine similarity approach but target different specific issues: O12 is about visualization granularity, A1 is about metric validity. Different author fixes needed.

edges.issue: Paper lacks causal analysis of inter-model homogenization mechanisms
edges.rationale: Both identify the same core gap: the paper diagnoses the Hivemind phenomenon but does not mechanistically disentangle causes (shared training data, alignment, decoding, memorization). A2 explicitly suggests comparing base vs instruction-tuned models; O3 similarly asks for disentangling pretraining vs alignment effects. Same complaint, same scope.

edges.issue: Need controlled experiments on base/foundation models to isolate causes of homogenization
edges.rationale: O15 specifically asks for experiments on foundation models without instruction-following to disentangle pre- vs post-training effects. A2 makes the same point more broadly ('comparing base models vs. their instruction-tuned variants'). O15 is one specific experiment that would partially address A2's broader call for causal analysis.

edges.issue: Section 4 human annotation analysis has fundamental methodological problems
edges.rationale: Both target Section 4's correlation analysis as methodologically flawed. O11 questions the subset selection methodology, entropy as disagreement measure, and averaging of human ratings. A3 flags the statistical artifact (reduced correlation from reduced variance) and small sample size. Different specific sub-complaints but both conclude Section 4's analysis is fundamentally problematic. Same author fix needed: proper null-model controls and alternative analysis methods.

edges.issue: Averaging human ratings as ground truth for correlation analysis is questionable
edges.rationale: O19 specifically questions why human ratings are averaged rather than accounting for annotator disagreement. A3's broader critique of Section 4 encompasses this (the 'reduced signal-to-noise ratio' argument directly relates to averaging noisy annotations). O19 is a specific sub-issue within A3's broader Section 4 critique.

edges.issue: Dataset construction lacks sufficient human validation
edges.rationale: O9 specifically targets the lack of human verification that queries are genuinely open-ended. A4 is broader — questions GPT-4o reliance for taxonomy labeling, query classification, AND open-endedness validation. A4 mentions the 3-annotator validation as limited, directly addressing the same issue as O9, but embeds it within a broader critique of automation reliance. Partial because A4 is broader and the specific complaint about open-endedness is one sub-point.

edges.issue: The paper's contribution may not be sufficiently novel or surprising
edges.rationale: Both question the significance of the contribution but from different angles. A5 says 'LM diversity loss is well-documented, this just scales up existing intuitions.' O4 argues from first principles that 'autoregressive LMs are designed to approximate average behavior, so cross-model similarity is statistically expected.' Same issue family (contribution significance) but different arguments: A5 is empirical precedent-based, O4 is theoretical/statistical. Partial because they share the conclusion (not novel enough) but differ in reasoning.

decision_drivers.text: Introduction of INFINITY-CHAT dataset and comprehensive open-ended prompt taxonomy fills a gap in studying language model output diversity.
Artificial Hivemind findings are well-supported by extensive empirical analysis across a large number of models and human annotations.

mentions.text: Paper addresses a critical issue in AI — the homogenization of language model outputs — with implications for AI safety and human creativity.
Methodology is robust, employing a large number of models and human annotations to ensure reliability of results.
Discussion on implications of homogenization for AI safety and human creativity is timely and relevant, potentially guiding future research.

agentic_concerns.text: The paper is dense with information, potentially overwhelming readers and obscuring main contributions; experimental setup sections could benefit from clearer, more concise presentation.
The dataset is limited to English-language queries, which may not capture the full diversity of global language use.
The study's focus on specific models and configurations might limit the applicability of the findings to other models or settings.
The paper could delve deeper into the underlying causes of the Artificial Hivemind effect, exploring the role of training data and model architecture.
The analysis of human annotations could be expanded to explore more nuanced aspects of human preferences and biases.
The paper's reliance on proprietary models and APIs may hinder reproducibility for researchers without access to these resources.
More detailed instructions on how to access and use the INFINITY-CHAT dataset would enhance the paper's utility for the research community.

edges.issue: Dataset is limited to English-language queries, constraining generalizability across languages and cultures
edges.rationale: Both identify the same specific limitation: INFINITY-CHAT contains only English queries from WildChat, which limits generalizability to other languages and cultures. Same scope, same normative conclusion.

edges.issue: Insufficient mechanistic analysis of why inter-model homogenization occurs
edges.rationale: Both flag the same gap: the paper diagnoses the Hivemind effect but does not mechanistically disentangle causes (training data, alignment, decoding). O3 is more specific (names contributing factors); A4 broadly says "could delve deeper into underlying causes, exploring role of training data and model architecture." Same underlying complaint.

edges.issue: Understanding why the Hivemind effect occurs and whether it is expected
edges.rationale: Both concern the lack of mechanistic understanding, but from different angles. A4 wants more analytical depth. O4 fundamentally challenges whether the finding is surprising given shared training data and the law of large numbers. A4 accepts the finding's significance and wants more explanation; O4 questions the contribution's value. Different normative implications.

edges.issue: Human annotation analysis methodology needs improvement
edges.rationale: Both target the Section 4 human annotation analysis. However, O11 identifies specific technical flaws (questionable subset selection, unjustified entropy metric, unclear averaging motivation) while A5 vaguely suggests the analysis "could be expanded to explore more nuanced aspects." The agentic system noticed the area but missed the specific technical problems. Severity gap of 2 levels (minor vs major) reflects the shallow critique.

edges.issue: Model coverage limitations may constrain generalizability of findings
edges.rationale: Both flag that the model selection limits generalizability. O15 specifically calls for testing on foundation models without instruction-following to disentangle pre/post-training effects. A3 broadly notes that focus on "specific models and configurations might limit applicability." Partial because A3's broader scope includes O15's specific concern, but fixing O15 alone (adding foundation models) would not fully resolve A3.

edges.issue: Dataset accessibility barriers for the research community
edges.rationale: Both concern the accessibility of INFINITY-CHAT. O14 specifically reports a broken dataset link at review time. A7 more broadly requests better documentation and instructions for accessing and using the dataset. Related family (data accessibility) but different facets: broken link vs documentation quality.

edges.issue: Presentation could be more concise
edges.rationale: Both flag conciseness concerns. O7 specifically targets Figure 1 as cluttered with too many models. A1 broadly flags the entire paper as dense and overwhelming, with experimental setup needing clearer presentation. Very different scope — fixing O7 (simplifying one figure) would not address A1's broader density concern.

mentions.text: The paper provides a thorough evaluation of LM output diversity and the Artificial Hivemind effect.
The paper effectively evaluates model alignment with human ratings.
The INFINITY-CHAT dataset is recognized as crucial for evaluating language model output diversity.

agentic_concerns.text: The paper needs more detailed analysis of how different decoding strategies (temperature, top-p, min-p) affect intra-model repetition and inter-model homogeneity, including systematic parameter comparisons.
The paper should conduct ablation studies to assess how variations in model architecture and training data influence alignment with human preferences.
The paper lacks detailed comparisons with existing methods and benchmarks, particularly regarding how INFINITY-CHAT improves upon previous benchmarks for evaluating LM diversity.
The criteria for selecting queries from WildChat, preprocessing steps, taxonomy construction assumptions, and annotation processes are not fully detailed.
The concept of the Artificial Hivemind effect needs a clearer definition and explanation of how it is systematically measured and identified.
The paper lacks specific details on model configurations, pre-training procedures, hardware/software specifications, and experimental conditions across 70+ models.
Evaluation metrics such as entropy and Spearman's correlation are used without providing specific formulas or methodological detail.
The dataset focuses on English-language prompts, limiting linguistic, cultural, and regional diversity and potentially constraining generalizability of findings.
Insufficient detail is provided for full study reproduction, including barriers from proprietary model access and incomplete specification of data collection to analysis pipeline.

edges.issue: English-only dataset limits generalizability across languages and cultures
edges.rationale: Both identify the same concern: the dataset uses only English-language prompts from WildChat, constraining cross-cultural and cross-linguistic generalizability. O1 severity=moderate, A8 severity=moderate.

edges.issue: Insufficient mechanistic understanding of what drives inter-model homogenization
edges.rationale: O3 asks for mechanistic disentangling of causes (shared training data, alignment, decoding). A1 asks specifically about decoding parameter effects on diversity. A1 is one narrow facet of the broader O3 concern. Both are aligned in wanting deeper causal understanding, but A1's scope is narrower.

edges.issue: Need to disentangle what model-level factors drive alignment and homogenization
edges.rationale: O3 requests mechanistic causal analysis of inter-model homogenization. A2 asks for ablation studies on model architecture and training data effects on human alignment. Both concern what drives convergent behavior, but O3 is about homogenization causes while A2 is about alignment quality. Partial because they share the same issue family (understanding model-level drivers) but target different outcomes.

edges.issue: Need experiments on model architecture/training variations to understand drivers of the effect
edges.rationale: O15 asks specifically for experiments on foundation models without instruction-following to determine whether post-training drives the effect. A2 asks for ablation studies on model architecture and training data effects on alignment. Both want more model-variation experiments, but O15 targets a specific comparison (base vs instruction-tuned) while A2 is broader. Partial match.

edges.issue: Data and code accessibility for reproducibility
edges.rationale: O14 flags a specific broken dataset link. A9 raises broader reproducibility concerns including data accessibility and proprietary model barriers. Same issue family (can others access the data?) but different specificity: O14 is concrete (broken link), A9 is general (sufficient documentation). Partial.

edges.issue: Code/data completeness for reproduction
edges.rationale: O16 asks for model-testing scripts in the codebase. A9 raises general reproducibility. Thematically related (both reproducibility) but different specific requests: scripts for each model vs overall pipeline documentation. Related, not partial — different author fixes needed.

edges.issue: Dataset construction methodology and validation
edges.rationale: O9 specifically asks for human validation that queries are genuinely open-ended. A4 asks for more detail about query selection criteria, taxonomy assumptions, and annotation processes. Both concern dataset construction methodology, but O9 targets a specific validation gap (are queries actually open-ended?) while A4 is about general methodological documentation. Different fixes needed — related only.

decision_drivers.text: Substantial empirical contribution: large-scale dataset, query taxonomy, and systematic evidence of mode collapse across language models, with the 'Artificial Hivemind' framing vivid and well-supported by core experiments.

mentions.text: The human annotation effort (31,250 labels with 25 annotators per example) is commendable and enables meaningful analysis of distributional preferences.

agentic_concerns.text: Section 4.3 text consistently names Pearson correlation but all figures (10, 11), captions, and tables (19, 23-26) report Spearman correlation coefficients, creating confusion about which statistical test was actually performed.

Percentage disagreement formula assigns 50% disagreement to unanimous tie annotations (all 25 annotators agree neither response is better), conflating consensus-on-tie with genuine preference disagreement, which affects downstream subset selection for the top-60% disagreement analysis.

Claim that inter-model similarity sometimes exceeds intra-model similarity is not well-supported by aggregate data; Tables 7-11 show diagonal (intra-model) values consistently exceed off-diagonal (inter-model) values, and the phrasing overstates what are at best instance-level occurrences as a more general pattern.

Abstract claims 6 top-level categories break down to 17 subcategories but only 15 are true subcategories; two top-level categories (Creative Content Generation, Brainstorm & Ideation) have no subcategories yet are counted as their own.

Figure 5 caption claims similarity 'typically exceeds 0.8' under min-p sampling but only 61.2% of cases do, overstating the robustness of mode collapse under diversity-oriented decoding and weakening the precision of the comparison with standard top-p settings (where 79% exceed 0.8).

edges.issue: Section 4 human disagreement analysis uses a flawed disagreement metric
edges.rationale: Both flag technical problems in the Section 4 disagreement analysis methodology. O11 is broader: covers subset selection methodology, entropy-based disagreement measure being unjustified, and unclear motivation for averaging human ratings. A2 identifies a specific formula flaw where P_disagree assigns 50% disagreement to unanimous ties. Both would require rethinking the disagreement metric, but A2 addresses only one sub-issue of O11's broader critique. Scope test fails for exact: fixing the P_disagree formula would not address O11's subset selection or averaging concerns.

edges.issue: Similarity score data does not support the interpretation given
edges.rationale: Both address how inter-model similarity data is interpreted and presented. O12 says scores are clustered in 0.7-0.8 with little differentiation, requesting full distributions rather than averages. A3 says the claim that inter-model similarity sometimes exceeds intra-model is not supported by aggregate data. Different specific complaints: O12 wants better visualization granularity; A3 wants a claim to be qualified. Different fixes. Related only because both critique the same figures/tables but from different angles.
